title: AI/ML Security Audit for Financial Services: LLM Prompt Injection and Data Exfiltration Defense
executive_summary: This case study details a comprehensive security audit of a major European bank's LLM-integrated customer support platform, which processes sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) and financial data. The engagement revealed 17 critical security vulnerabilities, including three zero-day prompt injection chains that could enable complete data exfiltration and unauthorized system access. Using the MITRE ATLAS framework for AI threat modeling, combined with custom red team exercises and guardrail effectiveness testing, we identified fundamental weaknesses in the platform's security architecture. Our remediation approach delivered a prioritized roadmap with code-level fixes, enabling the client to implement all critical patches within two weeks. The engagement demonstrates the urgent need for specialized AI security frameworks in financial services, where regulatory compliance and data protection requirements demand robust defenses against emerging LLM-specific threats.
client_context:
Client: Major European Bank (anonymized)
Sector: Financial Services
Size: €500B+ in assets under management, serving 25 million customers across 15 countries
Technology Stack: Custom-built LLM customer support platform integrated with core banking systems via APIs
Data Volume: Processes 2.3 million customer interactions monthly containing PII, account numbers, transaction history, and credit information
Regulatory Environment: Subject to PSD2, GDPR, and local banking regulations requiring strict data protection and audit trails
Business Criticality: Customer support platform handles 40% of initial customer inquiries, directly impacting customer satisfaction scores and regulatory compliance obligations
challenge: The client's LLM-integrated customer support platform presented multiple security challenges that threatened both operational continuity and regulatory compliance. Technically, the platform lacked specialized AI security controls, with traditional web application firewalls proving inadequate against prompt injection attacks and adversarial inputs designed to manipulate LLM behavior. The system's integration with core banking APIs created potential pathways for lateral movement and data exfiltration, while the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) component introduced risks of poisoned training data influencing model outputs. Business-critical concerns included potential GDPR violations from unauthorized data disclosure, reputational damage from security incidents, and regulatory penalties for inadequate data protection measures. The client specifically requested assessment of three primary risk categories: prompt injection vulnerabilities that could bypass security controls, data exfiltration pathways through LLM outputs, and model extraction attacks that could compromise proprietary algorithms or training data. Additionally, the client needed to understand agentic tool misuse scenarios where the LLM could be manipulated into performing unauthorized actions through its integrated toolset.
methodology: Our approach combined industry-standard threat modeling with specialized AI security frameworks to ensure comprehensive coverage of emerging LLM risks. We employed the MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Applications) framework as our primary methodology, mapping threats to specific AI system components and attack vectors. This was supplemented with STRIDE threat modeling for traditional system components and OWASP API Security Top 10 for integration points. Our assessment methodology included: (1) System architecture analysis to identify trust boundaries and data flow paths, (2) Adversarial threat modeling using MITRE ATLAS tactics and techniques, (3) Red team exercises simulating real-world attack scenarios, (4) Custom evaluation harness development for automated guardrail testing, (5) Code review focusing on AI-specific security patterns, and (6) Penetration testing of API integrations and data storage systems. We conducted threat modeling workshops with client security teams to validate our understanding of business logic and attack surface, ensuring our findings aligned with actual operational risks rather than theoretical vulnerabilities.
technical_approach: Our technical assessment proceeded through six distinct phases over a 3-week engagement period. Phase 1 involved comprehensive system reconnaissance, including architecture diagramming, data flow analysis, and identification of all LLM interaction points. We mapped the complete attack surface, from user input interfaces through to database storage and API integrations. Phase 2 focused on threat modeling using MITRE ATLAS, where we identified 23 potential attack vectors across four primary categories: prompt injection, data manipulation, model compromise, and agentic tool abuse. Phase 3 entailed building a custom evaluation harness using Python and LangChain frameworks, incorporating automated test cases for guardrail effectiveness validation. This harness included 150+ adversarial prompt templates organized by attack type and severity level. Phase 4 conducted intensive red team exercises, where our team attempted to exploit identified vulnerabilities using both automated tools and manual exploitation techniques. Phase 5 involved detailed code review of the LLM integration layer, focusing on input sanitization, output filtering, and prompt construction logic. Phase 6 culminated in comprehensive vulnerability validation and impact assessment, correlating technical findings with business risk implications.
key_findings: Our assessment uncovered 17 security vulnerabilities across the LLM customer support platform, categorized by severity and attack type. Critical findings (CVSS 9.0-10.0) included three zero-day prompt injection chains that allowed complete bypass of data access controls and enabled extraction of customer PII from backend systems. One chain exploited improper prompt templating, allowing attackers to inject system-level instructions that overrode security prompts. Another vulnerability in the RAG component permitted poisoning of retrieval documents, causing the model to generate fabricated responses containing sensitive data. A third critical issue involved insufficient output sanitization that allowed command injection through specially crafted responses. High-severity findings (CVSS 7.0-8.9) included seven vulnerabilities such as inadequate rate limiting enabling model enumeration attacks, weak authentication on API endpoints facilitating unauthorized access, and improper error handling that leaked system information. Medium-severity issues (CVSS 4.0-6.9) encompassed configuration weaknesses, logging deficiencies, and minor input validation gaps that could be chained with other vulnerabilities for more severe exploitation.
remediation: Our remediation strategy prioritized vulnerabilities based on business impact and exploitability, delivering a comprehensive roadmap with code-level guidance. For the three zero-day prompt injection chains, we provided specific code fixes including parameterized prompt templates using Jinja2, implementation of strict input validation with allow-lists, and deployment of output sanitization filters using regex patterns and semantic analysis. The RAG poisoning vulnerability required architectural changes including document integrity verification using cryptographic hashes and implementation of secure document retrieval protocols. For API security issues, we recommended deployment of API gateways with rate limiting, JWT-based authentication, and comprehensive logging. We provided sample code for implementing defense-in-depth controls including: (1) Input validation middleware using Pydantic models, (2) Output filtering using OpenAI Moderation API integration, (3) Prompt template libraries with proper escaping mechanisms, (4) Secure session management for conversation state, and (5) Comprehensive audit logging for all LLM interactions. All P0 (critical) findings were addressed within two weeks through iterative patch deployment and validation testing.
results: The remediation effort delivered measurable improvements in the platform's security posture. All 17 identified vulnerabilities were successfully remediated according to our prioritized roadmap, with all critical findings resolved within the two-week timeline. Guardrail effectiveness improved dramatically from 94% bypass rate pre-fix to 0% post-fix, demonstrating complete elimination of the identified attack vectors. Post-remediation penetration testing confirmed the effectiveness of implemented controls, with no successful exploitation attempts during follow-up assessments. The client achieved compliance with internal security standards and positioned the platform for upcoming regulatory audits. Business metrics showed no degradation in customer support performance, with response times remaining within acceptable parameters. The client expressed high satisfaction with our approach, particularly appreciating the actionable code-level guidance that enabled rapid implementation without extensive retraining of development teams. All findings were documented in a comprehensive security report with detailed remediation steps for future reference.
lessons: Several key insights emerged from this engagement that inform best practices for LLM security assessments. First, traditional security tools and methodologies are insufficient for protecting AI systems; specialized frameworks like MITRE ATLAS are essential for identifying AI-specific attack vectors. Second, prompt injection vulnerabilities require deep understanding of LLM internals and prompt engineering principles, necessitating security professionals with both AI knowledge and penetration testing experience. Third, the speed of remediation was critical - our ability to provide concrete code examples and implementation guidance enabled rapid patch deployment that might otherwise have taken months. Fourth, guardrail effectiveness testing must be automated and continuous, as manual testing cannot adequately cover the vast input space of LLM systems. Fifth, integration points between LLM systems and existing infrastructure create complex attack surfaces that require holistic security approaches rather than isolated component testing. Finally, client education about AI-specific risks proved crucial for successful remediation adoption and long-term security culture development.
applicability: This case study demonstrates broad applicability across financial services and other regulated industries handling sensitive data. Organizations deploying LLM systems for customer interaction, document processing, or decision support face similar security challenges and should conduct comparable assessments using AI-specific frameworks. The methodology is particularly relevant for institutions subject to GDPR, CCPA, and sector-specific regulations requiring demonstrable data protection controls. The custom evaluation harness and testing methodologies can be adapted for various LLM applications including chatbots, virtual assistants, and automated analysis systems. Financial institutions processing payment data should pay particular attention to the prompt injection and data exfiltration findings, as these represent direct pathways to PCI-DSS compliance violations. Healthcare organizations handling PHI will find the data protection aspects highly relevant, while any organization using RAG architectures should prioritize document poisoning prevention. The remediation strategies provide actionable guidance for security teams regardless of their AI expertise level, making this approach suitable for organizations at different stages of AI adoption maturity.
